name: Rosa Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays are lectures in software engineering and a lot of late nights in the lab, and on Saturdays I work the counter at a pharmacy near the market. On Sundays I sing in the church choir, which is the one thing that keeps me sane. I share a flat with two girls from my course, and my parents pay my rent while I cover the rest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to software engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grew up in a small farming town, and my dad repairs tractors for a living. He says every machine now has a computer in it, so someone in the family might as well understand the computer. My results were average, so I worked hard to get in. I use AI tools now and then, mainly to explain code that I can't follow, though I always check the answer myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, since new things always get oversold. I'd tell my flatmates to relax and keep studying. I'd say it quietly after choir to the older ladies who worry about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fine, because software is still a solid job and the world still needs people who understand it. My worry would be my parents' money, since farm repair work is seasonal and some winters are very thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my course and the pharmacy job. I'd look for a summer job in a software firm in the nearest city, even if it's unpaid for a few weeks. And I'd keep putting aside twenty pounds a month, for the winter months when my parents can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. I'm not someone who frets about the sky falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your worry in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter. My dad's work is slow from December to February, and my mum's small shop hours get cut. They'd never say it, but I can tell by how they stop talking about holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you do in a thin winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a Sunday shift at the pharmacy and ask for my share of the flat's heating to be split. I'd eat what my mum sends in boxes, and I'd smile when I tell her I'm fine.

say: I'd say it's about what I **expected**, since new things get oversold.
I'd tell worried older ladies at choir to relax.
think: Software is still a **solid** job and the world still needs people who understand it.
My parents' money is thin in winter, when repair work slows.
do: Keep the course and the pharmacy job, and look for a summer **software** job in the city.
Put aside twenty pounds a month for the thin winter months.
feel: I feel **calm**, since I'm not someone who frets about the sky falling.
S0.quote: I'd eat what my mum sends in boxes, and I'd smile when I tell her I'm fine.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **thin family winter** budget that she quietly protects.
Steady habits: uses AI for explanations, checks answers herself.
Hides money stress from her parents, like others in the group.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday counter job at the pharmacy
Look for a summer software job in the nearest city
Put twenty pounds a month into winter savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds like real change, and people should get ready for it, not complain. I'd say to my choir friends that machines have changed farming before, and people adapted. I'd not post online, I don't like the shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree is on the exposed side, because coding is one of the things named. But I also think someone must understand what's going on, and I'm the sort who checks things. Bosses will still want people they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more, like for testing and explaining, but I'd check every answer. I'd ask the pharmacy manager if he'd let me help set up his stock system, to build a real project. And I'd ask my dad if his workshop needs a simple booking program for repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but I can take it step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the booking program look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just a simple page where farmers book a repair slot and see the price. My dad writes everything in a paper diary, and people phone in and he forgets. A small thing, but it would show an employer I can build something that people use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably, if repair work gets done by machines that diagnose themselves. I'd say he should learn the diagnostic tools now, before he's forced to. He'd laugh, but then he'd try it, because he's practical.

say: I'd say people should **get ready** for this change, not complain.
I'd tell choir friends that machines changed farming before and people adapted.
think: Coding is named in the first wave, so my degree is **exposed**.
Bosses will still want people they trust, and I check things.
do: Use AI for testing and explaining but **check** every answer.
Build a simple repair booking page for my dad's workshop.
feel: I feel **concerned** but able to take it step by step.
S1.quote: My dad writes everything in a paper diary, and people phone in and he forgets.
fieldNote: She turns a worry into a **real project** for her father's workshop.
Practical, step-by-step, and trusts checking over hype.
Worries about her father's trade if machines diagnose faults.

steps.text: Build a simple repair booking page for her dad's workshop

Use AI to explain code, then check every answer herself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for ordinary families, and we need leaders to slow it down or help us. I'd say it after choir and to my parents at home. I'd keep my voice low, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my plan has collapsed. In two years I'd be in the middle of my degree, with thinking AI doing most of what I'm studying. My dad's trade lasts longer, until the robots arrive about 2031, but even that is only a delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home for a while, to be with my parents and work in the pharmacy full time. I'd ask my dad to teach me everything about the repair work, since hands-on work lasts longer. I'd stop spending anything beyond food and keep every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a stone in my chest, and I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years' warning do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would leave me with no good choice. If I keep studying, I use up my parents' money, but if I quit, I give up something I fought for. I'd probably stay for a term and then decide, but I'd hate every day of not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm coming home for Christmas and I'm not sure I'm going back. She'd say of course you are, and I'd say we'll see. I wouldn't want her to carry my worry too.

say: I'd say this is too **fast** for ordinary families and leaders must slow it down or help us.
I'd say it after choir and to my parents.
think: My plan has **collapsed**, with thinking AI doing most of my degree by the middle of it.
My dad's trade lasts until about 2031, but that is only a delay.
do: Go home for a while and work full time at the **pharmacy**.
Ask my dad to teach me the repair work and keep every pound.
feel: I feel **heavy**, like a stone in my chest, and I'd pray a lot.
S2.quote: If I keep studying, I use up my parents' money, but if I quit, I give up something I fought for.
fieldNote: Her **faith** and family anchor her, but two years leaves no good choice.
Would go home and learn her father's trade as a hedge.
Protects her mother from her worry.

steps.text: Move home for a term and work full time at the pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it well. I'd say churches and towns should help people prepare, not leave it to the government. I'd talk to my parents about money straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd have maybe two good years before the thinking AI takes over. It's tight, but not hopeless. And the robots for hands-on work come about three years after, so my dad's trade holds up a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement each summer, and learn a second skill like data for farms. I'd stay close to home and look for work with firms that serve farms. I'd keep saving and help my parents plan their finances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. A deadline is something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to run home. I can finish my degree and still help my parents, which feels right. Two years is a flood and five years is a bad winter, and you can prepare for a winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you advise your younger cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Mia is sixteen and wants to study history. I'd tell her to add a practical skill, like accounts or data, because thinking jobs go first. She'd roll her eyes, but I'd keep telling her.

I'd talk to my parents about money straight away.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with maybe two **good years** before thinking AI takes over.
My dad's trade holds up a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd tell people to work, save and look after neighbours. I'd also say politicians should plan with farmers and small towns, not only with city firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28, perhaps married, perhaps with a small company of my own. Ten years is long enough to build a life. The thinking AI would be part of the job, like a colleague I'd learned to trust slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a first job in the nearest city or a farm-tech firm, and save for a home. I'd keep singing in the choir wherever I live. And I'd try new AI tools as they become proven, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A bit of excitement, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The timing. Ten years could become six, and my parents might be older and less able to work. I'd keep an eye on their money and invite them to live nearby when it's right. Family is the real safety net, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently starting this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry less about my average marks and put more time into the choir and my friends. A career is long, and I'd rather have people around me than a perfect transcript.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and people should work, save and look after neighbours.
I'd tell politicians to plan with farmers and small towns.
think: By 2036 I could have a small **company** of my own and a settled life.
Thinking AI would be a colleague I learned to trust slowly.
do: Finish the degree, take a first job in a **farm-tech** firm and save for a home.
Try new AI tools only once they've been proven.
feel: I feel **calm** enough, with a bit of excitement.
S4.quote: Family is the real safety net, not the government.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep to **family and community** values and plan slowly.
Unease stays: her parents will be older and may need help.
Trusts AI only once proven, which suits her steady style.

steps.text: Take a first job in a farm-tech firm after graduating
Keep an eye on her parents' savings and plan to live nearby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Families like mine have no time to adjust, and my parents' money could be spent on a degree that may not pay. What would help is honest warning, local training that suits small towns, and firms in the countryside hiring young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm calmer than I might seem, because I trust my family and my faith. The change doesn't scare me as much as being on my own through it. I'd like to feel that my town will help me.

headlineQuote: I'm calmer than I might seem, because I trust my family and my faith.
portrait: Rosa is an **18-year-old** software engineering student from a farming town, working Saturdays at a pharmacy counter.
She is traditional and steady: faith, choir and family matter, and she uses AI tools now and then with checking.
Her father repairs tractors, so her fallback is hands-on and her **worry** is her parents' thin winters.
She is calm at plateau, alarmed at two years, and eased by five and ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, which forces a choice between her degree and her parents' money.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **warning**, local training suited to small towns and rural firms hiring young people.
